summary: Explains why congestion control is needed in the Internet and discusses what makes congestion control correct. It is a Best Current Practice document that guides designers of protocols and applications.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2914 explains why senders need to reduce their sending rate when the network is congested. It discusses how congestion control protects useful delivery and helps different flows share network capacity.

questions: why do udp flows need congestion control
subtitle: Why end systems must slow down when networks are congested, and how to judge congestion control.

tldr.problem: When network load rises but useful delivery falls, the network can suffer congestion collapse. Flows that do not respond to congestion can also use bandwidth at the expense of responsive flows.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains congestion collapse and fairness, defines a TCP-compatible flow, and discusses how the IETF should distinguish protocol rules from implementation details.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2914 is Best Current Practice 41. It sets out principles rather than defining a new congestion-control protocol, and the unit metadata lists RFC 7141 as an update.

sections.title: Why Congestion Control Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 2914 is a general discussion of congestion-control principles and the IETF's role in standardizing new mechanisms. Earlier IETF work focused on particular protocols, such as TCP and reliable multicast, or on how end systems and routers exchange congestion information.

The RFC says end-to-end congestion control is important for the stability of best-effort Internet traffic. Many applications do not use TCP, and some do not reserve bandwidth or use any end-to-end congestion-control method.

Congestion control for differentiated or integrated services is outside the document's scope where the network provides an end-to-end bandwidth guarantee.
sections.plainLanguage: When too much traffic competes for network capacity, senders need a way to respond. This RFC explains why that response matters for Internet stability.

sections.title: Congestion Collapse
sections.content:
Congestion collapse occurs when increased network load produces less useful work. The classical form described in the RFC involved TCP connections retransmitting packets that were already in transit or had reached the receiver. The RFC says timer improvements and TCP congestion control had generally corrected this form.

A second form occurs when bandwidth carries packets that are later dropped before reaching their destination. The RFC identifies this as a major unresolved danger, particularly when applications send without end-to-end congestion control.

End-to-end congestion control can reduce the sending rate when loss occurs. Another approach is a network guarantee that packets accepted at congested links will reach their destination. The RFC says the approaches can be combined.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can carry more packets but deliver less useful data if packets are repeatedly lost or discarded. Senders that reduce their rate during congestion help limit this waste.

sections.title: Fairness Between Flows
sections.content:
The RFC also considers fairness among best-effort flows. TCP connections can share a congested link reasonably equitably when they use compatible congestion-control algorithms. A flow that sends more aggressively can take bandwidth from other flows.

A flow is TCP-compatible if it responds to congestion notification and, in steady state under comparable conditions, uses no more bandwidth than a conformant TCP flow. The RFC distinguishes TCP-compatible flows, unresponsive flows and flows that respond to congestion but are not TCP-compatible. It says the last two classes pose significant threats to Internet performance.

Congestion control can also improve a flow's own performance. In some network conditions, a flow's sending rate affects the delay and loss it experiences.
sections.plainLanguage: Flows share a congested link more fairly when they respond to congestion in comparable ways. A TCP-compatible flow responds and does not use more bandwidth than comparable TCP traffic in steady state.

sections.title: Ways to Reduce Collapse and Share Capacity
sections.content:
The RFC does not require every best-effort flow to use TCP's Additive-Increase Multiplicative-Decrease method. To avoid collapse from undelivered packets, a flow needs to avoid maintaining a high sending rate when packet loss remains high.

Explicit Congestion Notification lets routers mark packets to report congestion instead of dropping them under moderate congestion. It does not remove the need to respond to congestion: when buffers overflow under heavy congestion, routers still have to drop arriving packets.

TCP-compatible methods can include rate-based versions of AIMD, AIMD with different parameters that give the same steady-state behavior, equation-based control using long-term loss information, and layered multicast where receivers join and leave groups.

Per-flow scheduling can provide fairness between flows, but the RFC says it cannot by itself prevent congestion collapse from undelivered packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Different algorithms can control sending rates. Whatever method is used, senders must avoid continuing at a high rate when congestion causes persistent loss.

sections.title: What the Standards Process Should Cover
sections.content:
The RFC says standards should cover aspects of a transport protocol that affect interoperability or are critical to performance. In TCP, reducing the congestion window after packet loss is such a mechanism. Implementation details that do not affect interoperability or significantly affect performance may not need standardization.

When considering a new transport protocol, the IETF should assess whether it has congestion control, how it performs and when it fails. A mechanism more aggressive than TCP faces a greater burden to show that it does not threaten network stability.

The RFC uses TCP examples to distinguish global concerns from local choices. Changing the initial window can affect congestion control across the network; choices such as rate-based pacing are described as not generally requiring standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: Standards should cover rules that affect how protocols work together or how they affect the whole network. Local implementation choices may not need a standard when they do not have those effects.

sections.title: Risks from Unresponsive Flows
sections.content:
This RFC discusses the risks of congestion control and of having no congestion control. It does not propose a specific mechanism, so it does not define specific security measures.

Individual mechanisms should resist attempts by endpoints to avoid responding to congestion. The RFC notes particular concerns for multicast, where receivers may fail to report congestion, and points to the risks posed by unresponsive flows.

The RFC says that subverting a few flows is a limited risk to the Internet as a whole. Widespread deployment of many endpoints that subvert congestion control poses the larger risk.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow that ignores congestion can harm other traffic. The larger risk comes when many endpoints behave this way, not just a few flows.
